summary: Aerobic respiration for ages 12–13: respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen, mainly in the mitochondria of living plant and animal cells, ALL the time (not only during exercise), producing carbon dioxide and water — word summary: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released). The defining goal is to separate respiration (the chemical release of energy inside cells) from breathing/ventilation (the muscular movement of air in and out of the lungs), and to explain why breathing and heart rate rise during exercise: faster breathing brings in more oxygen and removes more CO2, and a faster heart rate delivers more oxygen and glucose to, and carries more CO2 away from, respiring muscle cells. Keep it as a word summary, not a balanced symbol equation; do not yet require ATP or biochemical stages. Activities below include a driveable supply model, a consolidation and recognition check, a tap-to-reveal supply-chain image, a Socratic exchange, and a predict–observe–explain investigation with germinating vs boiled peas.
misconceptions: Believing respiration IS breathing — conflating cellular energy release with lung ventilation.
Thinking respiration only happens during exercise or only in the lungs — it occurs constantly in every cell's mitochondria.
Saying respiration 'makes' or 'creates' energy — energy is released/transferred from glucose, not created.
Thinking plants don't respire (only photosynthesise) — all living cells, including plant cells, respire all the time.
Assuming the purpose of breathing faster is to 'get rid of tiredness' rather than to supply more oxygen and remove more CO2 for respiration.

activities.title: Power a runner from the inside: driveable cell-and-body model
steps: Set an on-screen figure to rest or sprint and watch the zoomed-in muscle cell and its mitochondria below.
On 'sprint', raise breathing rate and heart rate (via sliders/controls) to keep oxygen and glucose flowing down the supply chain to the mitochondria.
Watch the mitochondrion 'engine' consume glucose and oxygen and release energy (shown as the legs doing work), plus CO2 and water as outputs.
Deliberately let supply fall behind demand and observe the energy gauge sag and the runner flag; then restore supply.

Read the labelled boundary that stays on screen: 'breathing = air in/out of lungs; respiration = this reaction in the cell', and note the reaction keeps running even when the figure just stands still.
Assemble the word equation from the glucose and oxygen flowing in and the CO2 and water flowing out.
activities.insight: Breathing (moving air at the lungs) and respiration (energy released by a reaction in the mitochondria) are different processes; respiration runs in every cell all the time, and exercise raises its rate so breathing/heart rate must rise to supply oxygen and glucose and remove CO2.

activities.title: Consolidate and check the key facts and misconception
steps: Complete a fill-in-the-blank of the word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released).
Decide for several short scenarios whether each describes breathing or respiration, and justify the choice.
Answer items on 'energy is released, not created' and 'all living cells respire, including plant cells'.
activities.insight: The word equation, the location (mitochondria), and the respiration-vs-breathing distinction are crisp, checkable facts the learner can state independently.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal supply chain: lungs → blood → cell → mitochondrion
steps: Tap each stage of a lungs-to-cell chain to reveal what is happening there.
Lift the flap on the lungs vs the mitochondrion to contrast 'breathing happens here' with 'respiration happens here'.
Reveal the word equation at the cell, tracing oxygen and glucose IN and CO2 and water out.
activities.insight: The players (lungs, blood, cell, mitochondrion) and the equation can be laid out explicitly, and the lungs-vs-mitochondrion contrast directly addresses the breathing/respiration confusion.

activities.title: Socratic exchange with an exercise physiologist
steps: Respond in role to an exercise physiologist asking 'Why are you panting after a sprint? Where does the energy actually come from?'
When tempted to say 'breathing gives energy', answer the follow-up: where does the reaction actually happen, and what is breathing for?

Reach the conclusion that extra breathing brings in more oxygen and removes more CO2, while a faster heart rate carries oxygen and glucose to respiring cells (and CO2 away), where the energy is released.
activities.insight: Articulating the reasoning out loud surfaces and corrects the breathing/respiration muddle through the learner's own explanation.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: germinating vs boiled peas
steps: Set up two vacuum flasks, each with a temperature probe and loosely plugged with cotton wool so air can get in: one with living germinating peas, one with peas that were boiled (dead) then cooled. Rinse both batches in dilute disinfectant first so microbes on the peas cannot respire and warm either flask.
BEFORE observing, predict which flask (if either) will warm up over a day, and explain WHY.
Over the day, record the temperatures and compare them with the prediction.

Explain the result: if the living peas warm while the boiled peas do not, that is evidence that respiration releases energy (some of it as heat) even in still organisms that do not breathe; relate this to 'every living cell, all the time'.
activities.insight: Respiration releases energy continuously in living cells, independent of breathing or exercise — a resting organism with no lungs or ventilation (germinating peas) is expected to warm because its cells respire, while the disinfected boiled-pea control should not.

checkQuestion: A footballer sits completely still on the bench, not moving at all. Are the cells in her body still respiring right now? Say yes or no — and tell me how you know.
checkAnswer: Yes — respiration happens in every living cell all the time, releasing energy from glucose using oxygen (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water) to keep the body working even at rest; it is not the same as breathing and does not switch off when she stops exercising.
